description: Building Marswalk Planner, our response to the NASA Space Apps Jakarta challenge Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map. It’s a layered map and planning tool that helps a Mars astronaut prepare and carry out a single surface excursion. The planner combines terrain and slope, thermal inertia, hydrated-mineral signatures and radiation dose.
summary:
TAPAK is a route planner for single crewed surface excursions on Mars. It pairs stochastic route planning with Damon, a biomechanical walking model fine-tuned from KINESIS for Martian conditions. Users set a base, science goals, and mission limits, and the app returns an optimized route with an oxygen budget, radiation dose, walk-back margin, and an explained GO, CAUTION, or NO-GO verdict.

To model Jezero Crater, TAPAK layers multiple NASA datasets: a 1-meter HiRISE terrain model and orthoimage, Perseverance MEDA temperature and pressure records, and a galactic cosmic ray dose model scaled by sky view.

Its core contribution is a physics-derived walking cost. Because standard energy models rely on unsuited humans in Earth gravity, TAPAK replaces them with costs learned from musculoskeletal simulations. Driven by the fine-tuned policy via reinforcement learning, an 80-muscle leg model traverses synthetic terrain patches under Mars gravity and spacesuit mass. A gradient-boosted surrogate then translates these results into per-step energy expenditure, fall probability, and stability metrics for the route search.
details:
What it does and how it works

TAPAK is a route planner for a single crewed walk on Mars, and its main feature is that it plans with biomechanics. Most planners pick the shortest or flattest path. We ask what it costs a suited astronaut's body to walk that path, and how likely the astronaut is to fall.

1. Biomechanics.

Standard walking-energy equations were fitted to people at Earth gravity without a pressure suit. We simulate the walking instead. An 80-muscle lower-body model (MyoLeg) in the MuJoCo physics engine walks over generated terrain patches. Each patch varies in:

- slope and cross slope

- roughness and rock density

- ground friction

- Mars or Earth gravity (3.711 m/s2 on Mars)

- suit and pack mass from 0 to 60 kg, with the pack's centre of mass shifted up, down and behind the torso

Each walk produces:

- the energy cost of walking

- whether the walker fell

- the stability margin (side to side and fore-aft)

- speed

We fine-tune a pretrained KINESIS walking policy with reinforcement learning (PPO). It was trained at Earth gravity with no load, so we adapt it to Mars gravity and a suit pack.

2. Machine learning model.

A gradient-boosted surrogate learns from these simulated walks. It takes 11 terrain, gravity and suit features and predicts four things: energy cost, fall risk, stability margin and speed. The predictions are exported as a slope-by-roughness lookup table with a fall probability per metre walked. The planner can then price any step in a fraction of a second and chain the steps into a probability of falling along a whole route.

3. Route search fused with the above.

A* and Dijkstra search runs on a 4 m grid built from a real 1 m HiRISE terrain model of the Jezero crater area. The cost of each step combines:

- the biomechanical energy and fall risk

- slope and roughness terms

- distance

- fatigue

Features on the WebApp (Which later be represented on astronaut tablet/Ipad)

1. EVA CHECKLIST

Consisting of before, during, and after the EVA. Astronaut also be able to chose presets that they created or sent by the base. There's also mission timeline highlighting events during EVA.

2. ROUTE PLANNER
Plans the walk before leaving the habitat. The astronaut sets the base, stops, science goals, and mission limits, and picks an efficient, balanced, or safest route style. The planner returns a route with distance, climb, steepest slope, oxygen, and radiation dose. It also shows a walk-back check and a GO, CAUTION, or NO-GO verdict with the reasons. Each step is priced by the biomechanics model for walking in Mars gravity with a suit pack, so the route is chosen for the astronaut’s body, not just the shortest line.

3. EVA MAP
The live map used during the walk. It shows the route and waypoints over real terrain, with four toggleable data layers: slope, hydrated minerals, thermal inertia, and radiation dose rate. A relay link margin layer can also be switched on. Hazard alerts flag steep slopes, boulders, radiation, and cold, and tell the crew what to do instead. A crew status panel tracks oxygen, power, dose rate, and comms link. The live telemetry is simulated and labelled as such.

4. FIELD-OF-VIEW SIMULATION
Shows what the astronaut will see on arrival at a stop (for example, “What to expect at WP3”), so the crew knows the ground and slope ahead before they get there. This screen currently uses placeholder imagery. We plan to replace it with real NASA surface images, with credit shown. Crew can also see satellite position which helps narrow beamwidth Ku/Ka-band ground stations (COTP/COTM unit) pointing. Manual pointing may occur during emergency.

5. COMMS (Link budget and Pass prediction)
Plans radio contact with the relay satellites. The pass prediction view lists each pass: when it rises and sets, its maximum elevation, and the uplink margin. A pass that is too low to hold the link is flagged. The link budget view uses a sky dome shaded by signal margin at each elevation. It also has a candlestick chart that follows the signal from transmitter to receiver, so the crew can see when the link could drop out. All values are modelled, not measured.

6. DEBRIEF
Review after the EVA. It compares the planned route with what happened, with measured values such as time, distance, oxygen, and dose, and lets the team log what to improve. The EVA playback and measured values are simulated in this prototype.

A return field computes the oxygen needed to walk home from every cell, so the route never goes where the crew could not get back. Mars weather (Perseverance MEDA) and a radiation dose model feed the same verdict, which is GO, CAUTION or NO-GO, with the reasons shown. Users choose an efficient, balanced or safest route style.
